Learned: Gradient boosting models (especially LightGBM) significantly outperform linear models on this dataset. Ratio features (weighted/non-weighted) capture meaningful relationships and improve performance. Tuning LightGBM (more trees, lower learning rate, regularization via subsample/colsample) further reduces error. Adding difference features did not help, possibly due to redundancy with ratio features or increased noise. CatBoost and XGBoost performed worse than LightGBM in our trials.

v1: val rmse 8.62233 (mean of seeds 1, 2, 3), from run e14: Tuned LightGBM with ratio features
## Works
- [m1] (tested on v0; val -9.1446; runs e14,e25,e26,e27) LightGBM (n_estimators=2000, lr=0.02, num_leaves=63, subsample/colsample=0.8) + ratio features (wtd/non-wtd) gives val RMSE ~8.62, huge gain over Ridge baseline 17.77.
- [m2] (tested on v0; val -9.0776; runs e9,e6,e19,e2) Gradient boosted trees (LightGBM/XGBoost) >> linear Ridge on superconductivity; ratio features improve tree models. Diff features don't help vs ratio.
## Failed
- [m3] (tested on v0; val -8.1572; runs e15,e11,e17) Linear Ridge (alpha 1.0 to 1e-4) stagnates at val ~17.75, no meaningful gain; CatBoost (~9.55) and feedforward NN (~15.3) underperform trees.
## Try next
- [m4] (tested on v0) Feature interactions (products of ratio features) or polynomial/log/sqrt transforms worth testing next for LightGBM.
- [m5] (tested on v0) Stacking/blending LightGBM+XGBoost+CatBoost, or stronger L1/L2 reg + early stopping (native callback) for LightGBM overfitting control.

Additionally, feature engineering (e.g., interactions) might help but given the feature richness, likely not necessary.

Best run: e50
Learned: Gradient boosting models performed best, with LightGBM slightly outperforming others. Linear and neural net models were much worse, indicating strong non-linear patterns. Increasing model capacity (more trees, more leaves, slightly lower learning rate) and using higher feature/bagging fractions improved validation RMSE from 8.674 to 8.603.
Next: With more runs, perform systematic hyperparameter tuning (e.g., Optuna) for LightGBM, explore feature interactions, or try stacking of top models.

Tried: XGBoost with ratio features (val 8.7762), CatBoost with ratio features (val 9.7981), MLPRegressor with ratio features and standardization (val 12.0739), LightGBM with ratio features, interaction features, and early stopping (val 8.8344), and original LightGBM with ratio features (val 8.6133).
Best run: e44
Learned: The original LightGBM with ratio features (no interactions, no early stopping) performed best among the tried models in seed 0 runs, achieving 8.6133 RMSE, slightly better than the previous best of 8.62233. Other gradient boosting models (XGBoost, CatBoost) performed worse, and neural nets underperformed. Interaction features and early stopping did not improve performance in this setting.
Next: Try multiple seeds to validate stability, test different random seeds for the LightGBM model, and consider feature selection or dimensionality reduction to potentially improve generalization. Also, experiment with different LightGBM hyperparameters (e.g., lower learning rate, more estimators) and other tree-based models like HistGradientBoosting.
